<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                <jats:p>
                  Computational drug-target interactions (DTI) prediction serves as a valuable tool for drug discovery and repurposing by cost-effectively narrowing down the potential drug-target space. This paper presents LinkDTI, a computational framework that predicts DTIs by identifying connections within a heterogeneous knowledge graph of drugs, proteins, diseases, and side effects. Unlike methods that rely on mathematical techniques like matrix completion or similarity-based scoring, LinkDTI uses an advanced graph-based approach to capture relationships between biomedical entities. Specifically, LinkDTI applies a modified version of the multilayer GraphSAGE model that learns from the heterogeneous knowledge graph and predicts potential drug-target interactions. Our model incorporates negative sampling that balances the data to address the issue of having more negative than positive interactions. Our results show that LinkDTI consistently performs better in AUROC and AUPRC than baseline methods by at least 2.5% across different sampling ratios and conditions. Subsequently, it identifies approximately 945 new potential DTIs, marking a 49.14% increase over known DTIs. Overall, LinkDTI offers a simple yet effective method for integrating diverse biomedical data to identify potential drug-target interactions. The code and data can be found at
                  <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="https://github.com/hub2nature/LinkDTI_heterogenous_KG.git">https://github.com/hub2nature/LinkDTI_heterogenous_KG.git</jats:ext-link>
                  .
                </jats:p>
title: LinkDTI: Drug-Target Interactions prediction through a Link Prediction framework on Biomedical Knowledge Graph

items.abstract: <jats:p>Persistent homology is increasingly used to build node and neighborhood features for graph learning. When those features are computed once on the full graph and then reused to predict individual edges, the feature of a node already encodes the very edge being predicted, and the reported accuracy is inflated. I quantify this target-edge leakage for topological link prediction across ten graphs, six real, including citation, coauthorship, and literary networks, and four synthetic, spanning scale-free, community, small-world, and spatial topologies. Under a protocol that removes each fold's test edges from the graph before any persistence feature is computed, apparent performance falls sharply and systematically: the mean inflation of the naive protocol is 0.11 AUC, reaches 0.20 on the citation graph, and on several graphs drops corrected singleparameter performance to chance, with a 95 percent confidence interval on the inflation that excludes zero. The inflation is present on all ten graphs and for both single-parameter and multiparameter features, and on a majority of graphs it reverses which of two methods appears better. As a controlled application of the protocol I compare single-parameter and multi-parameter fibered persistence, and find that once leakage is removed the multi-parameter advantage for edge prediction is small but statistically significant across the ten graphs, on the order of 0.01 to 0.03 AUC and concentrated where single-parameter persistence is weak. The reported performance of topological link prediction depends more on whether the protocol controls target-edge leakage than on the choice of persistence invariant, and I recommend the corrected protocol as a default for this literature.</jats:p>
title: Target-Edge Leakage Inflates Topological Link Prediction: A Quantification and a Corrected Protocol

items.abstract: Reliable AI-based early warning across courses requires risk probabilities that remain interpretable when learner behavior and outcome prevalence shift. Using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset, this study develops and evaluates a leakage-controlled cross-module framework that combines temporal behavioral profiling, zero-shot transfer, target-adaptive probability calibration, and capacity-constrained support prioritization. Models were assessed across 28 held-out module-cutoff combinations at days 14, 28, 42, and 56. Earlier presentations supplied learner-disjoint calibration samples covering 10%, 20%, or 30% of the historical target pool, while the chronologically latest presentation was reserved for final evaluation. At the 30% calibration level, the mean Brier score decreased from 0.243 to 0.205, negative log-likelihood from 0.708 to 0.599, expected calibration error from 0.158 to 0.076, and adaptive expected calibration error from 0.161 to 0.078. All seven module-level comparisons favored adaptation for each core metric, with bootstrap intervals excluding zero. Ranking performance was preserved because the selected mappings were predominantly monotonic. Importance weighting and source-side ensemble reweighting did not improve significantly beyond standard target calibration. The results show that modest historical target-domain data can substantially restore probability reliability under cross-course dataset shift and support more interpretable, capacity-aware review.
title: Target-Adaptive Probability Calibration for Reliable Student Risk Prediction under Cross-Module Dataset Shift

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
        <jats:p>Link prediction is a network analysis model used to discover missing links or future relationships that may appear, which has been widely used in many real network systems to predict the potential relationship between two individuals. However, link prediction can also be used by attackers to identify sensitive links that users are unwilling to expose, which makes only removing sensitive links from the original network ineffective and leads to the disclosure of privacy. In this paper, we propose a target link protection mechanism via artificial bee colony algorithm based on random walk (RABC), which can defend the link prediction attacks based on Resource Allocation (RA) metric effectively.To enhance the local search ability of RABC, the random walk algorithm is combined with the original artificial bee colony algorithm. Then, we compare our method with other existing methods, which shows that RABC has higher efficiency while ensuring the effectiveness. Finally, extensive experiments on real social networks are conducted to demonstrate the good performance of RABC on protecting sensitive links from being detected successfully by link prediction model. Furthermore, the perturbed networks generated by RABC is transferable to defend against other link prediction attacks.</jats:p>
title: Target Link Protection against Link-Prediction-Based Attacks via Artificial Bee Colony Algorithm Based on Random Walk

<jats:title>
                  A
                  <jats:sc>bstract</jats:sc>
                </jats:title>
                <jats:p>
                  MicroRNAs (miRNAs) and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) share Argonaute-mediated guide-target recognition, yet quantitative siRNA efficacy measurements are substantially scarcer and more costly to generate than miRNA-target interaction data. We therefore asked whether miRNA interaction data could provide transferable supervision for siRNA efficacy prediction. Here we present DuplexFM, a biologically grounded framework that uses sample-specific gates to integrate five evidence sources: pairing and sequence-context priors, duplex energetics, experimentally supervised mRNA accessibility, target-to-guide cross-attention, and contextual token-pair compatibility. The accessibility expert, trained on nucleotide-resolution icSHAPE measurements, achieved a held-out nucleotide-level Pearson correlation of 0.627 and evaluated accessibility at seed match and energy-supported candidate sites. On miRBench v7, three independently trained DuplexFM models achieved a macro APS of 0.873±0.002, soft-voting increased this to 0.876 and yielded the highest APS on all four test sets. We then froze the miRNA-trained representation and trained only a lightweight residual head with 24 siRNA-specific descriptors. Transfer improved Pearson and Spearman correlations, AUPRC, and F1 over the descriptor-only baseline in all six evaluation settings. The ensemble achieved the highest Pearson and Spearman correlations in four settings, whereas OligoFormer remained stronger on Huesken and Takayuki. These findings show that experimentally grounded accessibility and miRNA-derived interaction representations provide complementary, transferable information, supporting a parameter-efficient route towards unified modeling of Argonaute-guided RNA regulation. Code and data are available at
                  <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="https://github.com/cbaiming/DuplexFM">https://github.com/cbaiming/DuplexFM</jats:ext-link>
                  .
                </jats:p>
title: DuplexFM: Transferable small-RNA target representations link miRNA interactions to siRNA efficacy prediction

items.abstract: Conformal prediction quantifies uncertainty without parametric outcome assumptions, but standard coverage relies on exchangeability. Importance weighting can restore validity under covariate shift when density ratios are known. In deployment, practitioners often have labeled source data and only unlabeled target covariates, raising a basic question: can those data determine whether coverage remains credible? We introduce DriftGuard, a two-stage audit. Its label-free stage reports domain discriminability, effective sample size of estimated density ratios, weight stabilization, and visible abstention. We establish exact and approximate detectability bounds, a minimax testing consequence, and a sharp $[0,1]$ identified set for target coverage under unrestricted conditional shift. DriftGuard-L crosses this boundary with a probability sample of target labels, using an exact one-sided coverage test, prospective label-budget calculation, and finite-sample conformal recalibration. Under strong Gaussian covariate shift, ordinary conformal coverage fell to 0.789, while oracle and cross-fitted weighted conformal prediction attained 0.926 and 0.923. A published doubly robust comparator was robust when either nuisance was oracle, whereas both-misspecified coverage fell to 0.812. In an untouched chronological deployment of 8,734 hourly Bike Sharing observations, source conformal, estimated weighting, and estimated doubly robust calibration undercovered (0.568--0.594); 2,176 delayed target labels raised subsequent coverage from 0.558 to 0.884. Under pure concept shift, an overlap score remained near 0.96 while coverage fell from 0.90 to 0.40. Exact label budgets quantified power, and target recalibration restored synthetic evaluation coverage. The framework separates overlap diagnosis, visible abstention, target-label falsification, and repair.
title: Auditing Conformal Prediction under Distribution Shift: A Detectability Boundary, Exact Label-Budget Design, and Repair
